newsitem.title: USA: Clinton sees budget hope, Lott seeks "bold move".
newsitem.headline: Clinton sees budget hope, Lott seeks "bold move".

text.p: President Clinton said Friday he sees new hope for reaching a budget accord with the Republican-led Congress, but the Senate's top Republican said the president needs to make "a really bold move" if he wants to reach a deal.

At a White House news conference Clinton said the bipartisan cooperation that led to Senate approval of the chemical weapons treaty Thursday convinced him that a balanced-budget accord is also attainable and "we will do it."
He said he would like to see an agreement soon but if that were not possible, would recommend the two sides keep talking.
"It would be so good for our economy. It would keep interest rates down. It would keep job growth growing," Clinton said of balancing the budget.

White House officials have been negotiating with senior Republican and Democratic lawmakers to work out very deep differences over the size of tax cuts and spending cuts that should be adopted in a five-year balanced budget.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott said Republicans were continuing negotiations with the administration, but if no agreement were reached soon he would move a budget proposal being worked out with conservative Democrats.

Republicans made a proposal that moved in the direction of the White House on the size of proposed tax cuts and on Medicare spending reductions, but were still far from the president's proposal. Lott said they were awaiting a reply offer.
At a news conference in his Senate office, Lott urged the president to make a "bold move" on the budget front this weekend when he talks on television about volunteerism.
"I hope he won't just talk about volunteerism but will also talk about some really bold move on the budget," Lott said.

"I think progress is being made. There is movement on both sides, I think in the right direction. There is still a signficant gap. But I have been saying to both sides it is time to stop holding back now," Lott said of the budget talks.

While all sides have said there has been enough progress during the closed door negotiations to warrant continued efforts, other lawmakers outside the inner budget circle have expressed growing concerns that the final deal is moving away from what they want.

Senate Finance Committee chairman Bill Roth, Republican of Delaware, asserted his right to draft tax policy in his panel. In a letter to Lott, he said he viewed a net $143 billion tax cut over five years as the bare minimum that should be included in the budget.
Clinton has sought a $98 billion tax cut through 2002 offset by $76 billion in other tax increase for a net tax cut of $22 billion.
"In order to provide both family tax relief and promote long term economic growth, the net tax cut must be significant and larger than the press reports of $80 billion," Roth wrote.
"My view is that roughly $143 billion in net tax cuts over five years is really the bare minimum..." he said.

Roth said net savings of $115 billion to $120 billion in Medicare would be "much more realistic" than the reported $130 billion in net savings under discussion. Clinton has said $100 billion in Medicare savings over five years is enough to keep the programme on sound financial footing.
